name: ACL
syntax: ACL GETUSER user | SETUSER user [on] [>secret] [+cat ...] [-cat ...] | DEL user
summary: Adds, removes and configures users. ACL data is stored apart from the main data and is not replicated. It is available only on the RESP interface, by default port 14000. The special flag all grants or removes every permission at once.
example:
ACL SETUSER krease on >test123 +read +write +keys +hash
OK
ACL GETUSER krease

name: ADD
summary: Adds a key only if it is not already there. An existing key is left alone, but the reply is OK either way, so you cannot tell whether the value was stored. Use SET NX if you need to know.
example:
ADD n1 v
+OK
ADD n1 v2
+OK      # not stored; n1 is still v

name: ADDROUTE
summary: Adds a destination that write commands in the data category are forwarded to. Routes are held per key space.

name: APPEND
summary: Adds bytes to the end of the stored value, creating the key if it is missing. A compressed value is decompressed, written, and stored back uncompressed so the dictionary is not run on every append.

name: AUTH
summary: Authenticates the connection. The default user is already authenticated when a connection opens, and if no rights were ever set it holds all of them. Changing the default password without care leaves no usable connection, because AUTH can no longer succeed. Safer: ACL SETUSER default -all +auth.

name: BLMOVE
syntax: BLMOVE source destination LEFT|RIGHT LEFT|RIGHT timeout
summary: What LMOVE does, waiting up to timeout seconds when the source is empty. The timeout is the same check BLPOP uses. 0 waits until something arrives.
example:
RPUSH src a
:1
BLMOVE src dst RIGHT LEFT 1
$1
a

name: BLMPOP
syntax: BLMPOP timeout numkeys key [key ...] LEFT|RIGHT [COUNT count]
summary: What LMPOP does, waiting up to timeout seconds when every named list is empty. The timeout is checked before any lock is taken; a hex or overflowing number is refused. 0 waits until something arrives.
example:
RPUSH l a
:1
BLMPOP 1 1 l LEFT
*2
$1
l
*1
$1
a

name: BLPOP
summary: Removes an entry from the high end of the list, waiting up to timeout seconds if the list is empty. Only one blocking wait may be set on a key at a time; a second is refused.

name: BRPOP
summary: Removes an entry from the low end of the list, waiting up to timeout seconds if the list is empty. Only one blocking wait may be set on a key at a time; a second is refused.

name: BRPOPLPUSH
summary: BLMOVE source destination RIGHT LEFT timeout.
example:
RPUSH src a
:1
BRPOPLPUSH src dst 1
$1
a

name: BZMPOP
syntax: BZMPOP timeout numkeys key [key ...] MIN|MAX [COUNT count]
summary: What ZMPOP does, waiting up to timeout seconds when every named set is empty. The timeout is the same check BLPOP uses. ZADD wakes a waiter.
example:
ZADD z 1 a
:1
BZMPOP 1 1 z MIN
*2
$1
z
*1
*2
$1
a
$1
1

name: CALLF
summary: Run the stored function name and reply with what it returned. Arguments arrive as a 1-based array of strings; the command name and the function name are not among them. A missing function is an error. The function is also reachable as a command in its own right once the builtin table has missed, and space:NAME reaches one in another space. CALLF is a read as far as ACL is concerned; writes the script makes go through barch.call and barch.store, which check the caller's rights.
example:
SETF greet "function call(who) return \"hello \" .. who end"
+OK
CALLF greet world
$11
hello world
greet world
$11
hello world
CALLF nosuch
-ERR no such function

name: CLEARALL
summary: Empties every key space. Destructive, and in the dangerous ACL category.

name: CLIENT
syntax: CLIENT LIST | INFO | SETNAME name | GETNAME | CLEAR_ITERS
summary: Reports and adjusts connection state. LIST describes every connection in the Redis format; INFO describes this one, including iters and iters-mem for open SCAN cursors. CLEAR_ITERS releases the cursors this connection is holding.

name: CONFIG
syntax: CONFIG GET name | CONFIG SET name value | CONFIG RESETSTAT
summary: Reads and writes server configuration at runtime. Every option can be changed without a restart. Redis configuration names are accepted alongside the native ones. ordered_keys is the default store for new spaces: the ART when true, an unordered hash when false. Per-key-space options are read once when a space is first built, so changing those needs the space to be reopened.

name: COPY
summary: Copies a value to a second name, leaving the source alone. Without REPLACE an existing destination is refused and the reply says so.
example:
SET a 1
+OK
COPY a b
:1
COPY a b
:0
COPY a b REPLACE
:1

name: COUNT
summary: Counts keys between two bounds without returning them. The count is exact. An empty or inverted range is not an error; it counts as zero. A bound is held to the same rule as a key: it may not contain a NUL except as a trailing terminator, which is taken as one and removed. An interior NUL is refused rather than silently matching nothing.

name: DBSIZE
summary: The same handler as SIZE, under Redis's name.

name: DECR
summary: Reads the value as a signed 64-bit integer and subtracts one. A missing key is created at -1. A non-integer is left as it was and the reply is an error.

name: DECRBY
summary: Reads the value as a signed 64-bit integer and subtracts the given amount. A missing key is created at the negated amount. A non-integer is left as it was and the reply is an error.

name: DEL
summary: Removes one or more keys and replies with how many were actually removed. Missing keys count as zero. This is Redis DEL. REM is the barch spelling that replies with the removed value.

name: DIR
syntax: DIR LS|COUNT|RM path [SEP s] [AFTER name] [OFFSET n] [LIMIT n] | DIR MV|CP path to [SEP s]
summary: Plain keys walked as a tree, split on a separator - `:` by default, which is what LOADKEYS writes. There is no metadata behind it, unlike FS: a key such as `a:b:c` makes `b` a child of `a` that is also a node. LS lists one level, each child once, and jumps past everything under it. OFFSET leaves out that many children first; they are stepped over rather than read, and it only applies to LS. COUNT counts every key under the path, RM removes them, and MV and CP move or copy the whole subtree.
example:
DIR LS a
key 3 k001
node 0 sub
DIR LS a OFFSET 100 LIMIT 20
DIR COUNT a

name: EXEC
summary: Runs the commands queued since MULTI and returns their replies in order.

name: EXISTS
summary: Counts how many of the named keys exist. A key given twice counts twice, as in Redis.

name: EXPIRE
summary: Sets a time to live in seconds on an existing key. A missing key is not an error; the reply is -1. The condition flag is read from a fixed position; an unrecognised word there is ignored.

name: EXPIREAT
summary: Sets the expiry to a unix time in seconds. A time that has already passed deletes the key.

name: EXPIRETIME
summary: When the key will expire, as a unix time in seconds. The deadline is rebuilt from the remaining time against the system clock, so a clock jump moves every expiry. See the warning on expiry and restarts.
example:
SET a 1
+OK
EXPIREAT a 1893456000
:1
EXPIRETIME a
:1893456000

name: EXPORT
summary: Writes the current key space to a file as the commands that would rebuild it — SET for a plain value, HSET, RPUSH and ZADD for the collections — not as a copy of the pages. A shard file records the format it was written with and a server refuses one it does not recognise, so a page copy stops being readable the moment the format changes. Commands land on any build that has those commands. An expiry travels as an absolute PXAT, so a slow export does not quietly shorten every deadline. The file is a RESP command stream, binary-safe, and can be replayed by anything that speaks the protocol, including redis-cli --pipe, not only by IMPORT.
example:
SET a 1
+OK
HSET h f v
:1
EXPORT /tmp/space.resp
:2

name: FIRST
summary: The first key at or after the one given, in key order. An alias of LB, kept because it reads better when walking a range.

name: FLUSHALL
summary: Empties every key space, as Redis FLUSHALL does. FLUSHDB stays on the selected space. Destructive, and in the dangerous ACL category.

name: FLUSHDB
summary: Empties the currently selected key space. FLUSHALL is the one that reaches every space. Destructive, and in the dangerous ACL category.

name: FS
syntax: FS LS path [AFTER name] [OFFSET n] [LIMIT n] [SOURCE] | STAT path | GET path [FROM off] [LEN n] | FETCH path | PUT path content [TYPE t] [CHUNK n] [RELOAD] | RM path | MV path to | CP path to | MKDIR path | RMDIR path [RECURSIVE]
summary: The file store of the current space, one command for reading and writing both. A file is three kinds of key - a name record, an inode and its chunks - so everything here is ordinary key access and the same ACL applies; there is no second permission system for files. One command covers both halves, which means the categories are the widest of what it can do and a read-only caller cannot have FS at all. LS walks one level, not the tree. FETCH is a verb of its own rather than something GET does quietly, because a space with a source may go to the network to answer it. Options come in pairs, so a word left over at the end is an error.
example:
FS LS /files
file 6 1 a.txt
dir 0 0 sub
FS LS /files OFFSET 1 LIMIT 10
dir 0 0 sub
FS STAT /files/a.txt
path=/files/a.txt kind=file size=6 chunk=65536 chunks=1 version=1 type=text/plain
FS GET /files/a.txt
hello
FS PUT /x.txt "some bytes" TYPE text/plain
:1
FS RM /x.txt
:1

name: FUNCTIONS
syntax: FUNCTIONS SYNC [repo] [commit] | STATUS | COMMANDS | CRON | QUEUES
summary: Apply stored-function repositories, or report on them. SYNC with nothing applies every enabled repository. One extra argument is a repository name if it is one, otherwise a commit to pin this apply to. Two extra arguments are the repository and the pin. A broken file refuses the whole apply and leaves the previous functions in place. STATUS is one line per repository (or "no repositories"). COMMANDS lists what the current space exposes as RESP commands: the name, the function key that defines it, and its ACL categories. CRON lists scheduled jobs. QUEUES is the same as QUEUE STATUS.
example:
FUNCTIONS STATUS
no repositories
FUNCTIONS SYNC
+OK
FUNCTIONS COMMANDS
1) "GETNAME NAMER read"
2) "SETNAME NAMER write,data"

name: GET
summary: Reads the value stored at a key. A missing key is not an error; the reply is nil.

name: GETDEL
summary: Reads the value and deletes the key in one step. A missing key replies nil and deletes nothing. There is no conditional form. A key holding a collection is left alone.
example:
SET s v
+OK
GETDEL s
$1
v
GET s
$-1

name: GETEX
syntax: GETEX key [EX s | PX ms | EXAT unix-s | PXAT unix-ms | PERSIST]
summary: Reads the value and can change its expiry at the same time. With no option the expiry is left as it is. PERSIST removes it; EX, PX, EXAT and PXAT set a new one. A bad expiry is refused.
example:
SET g v
+OK
GETEX g EX 100
$1
v
TTL g
:100
GETEX g PERSIST
$1
v
TTL g
:-1

name: GETF
summary: The stored source for name, or null when there is no such function. The name folds to upper case, so GETF greet and GETF GREET are the same key. GET cannot read a function key; this is the command that can.
example:
SETF greet "function call() return 1 end"
+OK
GETF greet
$28
function call() return 1 end
GETF nosuch
$-1

name: GETRANGE
summary: The bytes between two positions, both ends included. Positions start at 0; a negative counts back from the end, so 0 -1 is the whole value. Positions past either end are clamped. A missing key replies with an empty string, not nil, so an empty reply does not tell you the key was missing. A key holding a collection is the wrong type.
example:
SET s "Hello World"
+OK
GETRANGE s 0 4
$5
Hello
GETRANGE s -5 -1
$5
World

name: GETSET
summary: Sets a key and replies with what it held before. A missing key replies nil and is created. Redis prefers SET with GET, which barch also accepts.
example:
SET a 1
+OK
GETSET a 2
$1
1
GET a
$1
2

name: GRAPH
syntax: GRAPH LS path [AFTER edge] [OFFSET n] [LIMIT n] | STAT path [EDGE id] | GET path [FROM off] [LEN n] [EDGE id] | PUT path content [TYPE t] [CHUNK n] | MKDIR path | LINK node-id path | UNLINK path [EDGE id] | RM path [RECURSIVE] [EDGE id] | MV path to [EDGE id] | CP path to [TYPE t] [CHUNK n] | BFS start [DEPTH n] [OFFSET n] [LIMIT n] | DFS start [DEPTH n] [OFFSET n] [LIMIT n]
summary: The graph store of the current space: a file store where a path is a chain of edges. Each edge gives a node a name under a parent node, and one node can have edges from several parents, so the same file or directory can answer at several paths. Directories hold edges and leaves hold bytes, stored the same way FS stores a file. LINK adds an edge to a node that already exists, and PUT to a linked leaf changes it at every path. UNLINK removes one edge, together with anything that edge was the last route to. RM removes the node and every edge naming it. A directory can be linked under itself or its own subtree; the walks list each node once, and UNLINK and RM clean up a cycle nothing else reaches. When a directory has two edges with the same name, a path takes the oldest, and EDGE picks another by its id. CP copies a directory whole, in the same shape: a node shared inside it stays shared inside the copy. Like FS, one command covers reading and writing, so a read-only caller can't use GRAPH, and options come in pairs, so a word left over at the end is an error.
example:
GRAPH MKDIR /docs
+OK
GRAPH PUT /docs/a.txt hello TYPE text/plain
+OK
GRAPH STAT /docs/a.txt
path=/docs/a.txt kind=leaf id=3 refs=1 edge=4 size=5 chunk=65536 chunks=1 version=1 type=text/plain
GRAPH LINK 3 /shared.txt
+OK
GRAPH LS /
dir 2 1 1 docs
leaf 5 3 2 shared.txt
GRAPH GET /shared.txt
hello
GRAPH BFS /
0 /
1 /docs
3 /shared.txt
GRAPH UNLINK /shared.txt
+OK
GRAPH CP /docs /backup
+OK
GRAPH RM /docs
-ERR /docs is not empty
GRAPH RM /docs RECURSIVE
+OK

name: HDEL
summary: Removes fields from a hash. Missing fields are skipped. The reply is how many were actually removed.
example:
HDEL h f1
:1
HDEL h nope
:0

name: HELLO
summary: Negotiates the protocol version for the connection and reports the server's details. Versions 2 and 3 are both served; anything else is refused with NOPROTO. The AUTH form runs the ordinary AUTH command and takes its OK back, so the handshake is all the client sees.

name: HEXISTS
summary: Whether a field is present in a hash.
example:
HEXISTS h f1
:1
HEXISTS h nope
:0

name: HEXPIRE
syntax: HEXPIRE key seconds FIELDS numfields field [field ...]
summary: Sets a time to live in seconds on named fields. Missing fields are reported per field in the reply; they do not fail the call.

name: HEXPIREAT
syntax: HEXPIREAT key unix-time FIELDS numfields field [field ...]
summary: As HEXPIRE, but the expiry is an absolute unix time.

name: HEXPIRETIME
summary: The absolute expiry time set on named fields. It takes the FIELDS form like the other per-field hash commands.

name: HGET
summary: Reads one field from a hash. A missing field, or a missing hash, replies nil.
example:
HGET h f1
$2 v1
HGET h nope
$-1

name: HGETALL
summary: Every field and value in the hash, as a flat sequence of field, value, field, value. A missing hash replies with an empty array.

name: HGETDEL
summary: Reads named fields and removes them in one step. The FIELDS form is required; HGETDEL key field is refused.

name: HINCRBY
summary: Adds an integer to a hash field, creating the field at that amount if it is missing. A non-integer field is left as it was and the reply is an error.
example:
HINCRBY h ctr 3
:3
HINCRBY h ctr 3
:6

name: HINCRBYFLOAT
summary: Adds a floating-point amount to a hash field, creating the field at that amount if it is missing. A non-number field is refused, and so is an increment of NaN or infinity.

name: HKEYS
summary: The field names in the hash, without their values. A missing hash replies with an empty array.

name: HLEN
summary: How many fields are in the hash. A missing hash replies 0.

name: HMGET
summary: Reads several fields at once. Missing fields come back as nils in the same positions, so the reply always has one entry per field.

name: HMSET
summary: Sets fields on a hash and always replies OK. This is the older name for HSET; Redis still uses it in a lot of its own tests. A key that already holds a string or another collection is refused.
example:
HMSET h a 1 b 2
+OK
HLEN h
:2

name: HRANDFIELD
summary: Picks a field at random. With no count, one field comes back, or nil if the hash is missing. A positive count asks for that many distinct fields; a negative count allows repeats. The reply is built in memory first, so a count past a million is refused. Redis streams and has no such limit.
example:
HMSET h a 1 b 2 c 3
+OK
HRANDFIELD h
$1
b
HRANDFIELD h 2 WITHVALUES
*4
$1
a
$1
1
$1
b
$1
2

name: HSCAN
summary: Walks the fields of one hash a page at a time. Start with cursor 0 and pass back the cursor each reply carries until it comes back as 0. A full iteration reports every field that is present throughout it. A field added or removed while it runs may or may not appear, and a field may be reported twice — the same promises SCAN makes over a key space. A cursor the server no longer recognises starts again from the beginning.

name: HSET
summary: Stores one or more fields in a hash, creating it if needed. The reply counts fields that were new, so you can tell an insert from an update. An odd number of field/value arguments is a wrong-arity error.
example:
HSET h f1 v1 f2 v2
:2
HSET h f1 other
:0

name: HSETNX
summary: Sets one field only if it is not already there. An existing field is left alone and the reply is 0.
example:
HSETNX h a 1
:1
HSETNX h a 9
:0
HGET h a
$1
1

name: HSTRLEN
summary: How long a field's value is, in bytes. A missing field replies 0, same as STRLEN on a missing key, so you cannot tell an empty value from an absent one with this command alone.
example:
HSET h a hello
:1
HSTRLEN h a
:5
HSTRLEN h nope
:0

name: HTTL
summary: How many seconds are left on named fields. The FIELDS form is required; HTTL key field is a syntax error.

name: HVALS
summary: Every value in the hash, in the same field order as HKEYS.
example:
HMSET h a 1 b 2
+OK
HVALS h
*2
$1
1
$1
2

name: IMPORT
summary: Replays an export into the current key space. It merges: names in the stream are overwritten and everything else is left alone, so clearing the space first is your decision. Each command is run through the ordinary command path, so a stream from an older build lands here as long as this build has the commands — and stops with an error naming the command if it does not. Replies from the replayed commands are not returned; the reply is a count.

name: INCR
summary: Reads the value as a signed 64-bit integer and adds one. A missing key is created at 1. A non-integer is left as it was and the reply is an error.

name: INCRBY
summary: Reads the value as a signed 64-bit integer and adds the given amount. A missing key is created at that amount. A non-integer is left as it was and the reply is an error.

name: INCRBYFLOAT
summary: Adds a floating-point amount to a key, creating it at that amount if it is missing. A non-number is left as it was, and so is an increment of NaN or infinity. The result is stored in the same form it is replied in, so reading it back gives the same digits.

name: INFO
summary: Reports server information for a named section — memory, commandstats, replication and the rest. Bare INFO, the form every client sends on connect, is not implemented and replies with an error. INFO SHARD #n reports one shard, and needs three separate protocol arguments.

name: KEYSF
summary: The function names in this space, in their canonical (folded) form, sorted. An optional glob filters the list the way KEYS does. This is a range walk over the function keys, not a scan of the whole space.
example:
SETF greet "function call() return 1 end"
+OK
SETF counter "function call(...) return select(\"#\", ...) end"
+OK
KEYSF
1) "COUNTER"
2) "GREET"
KEYSF GR*
1) "GREET"

name: KSOPTIONS
summary: Reads or sets an option on the current key space. ORDERED ON keeps keys in the ART; ORDERED OFF uses the unordered hash. That overrides the global ordered_keys default for this space only. Options set this way are saved in the space's shards, not in the configuration space.

name: KSPACE
syntax: KSPACE DEPENDS dep ON source [STATIC] | RELEASE dep FROM source | DEPENDANTS name | DROP name | MERGE dep [TO target] | OPTION [SET|GET] ORDERED|LRU|RANDOM [value] | EXIST name
summary: Administers key spaces and the layering between them. A dependent space resolves its misses in its sources; keys written to it stay there. MERGE folds a dependent into its sources; RELEASE detaches one. Both spellings, dependent and dependant, are accepted.
example:
KSPACE DEPENDS overlay ON base
KSPACE MERGE overlay
KSPACE EXIST overlay

name: LB
summary: The first key at or after the given one. Replies nil if nothing sorts there or later.

name: LBACK
summary: Reads the entry at the high end of the list without removing it. A missing or empty list replies nil. LPUSH and RPUSH are reversed relative to Redis, so the back is the opposite end from the one a Redis user would expect.

name: LCS
summary: The longest common subsequence of two values. Characters must appear in order, but they do not have to be next to each other. Plain form replies with the subsequence; LEN replies with its length; IDX replies with match ranges. Memory is the product of the two lengths, so large values cost.
example:
SET k1 ohmytext
+OK
SET k2 mynewtext
+OK
LCS k1 k2
$6
mytext
LCS k1 k2 LEN
:6
LCS k1 k2 IDX MINMATCHLEN 4
1# "matches" => 1) 1) 1) (integer) 4
         2) (integer) 7
      2) 1) (integer) 5
         2) (integer) 8
2# "len" => (integer) 6

name: LENGTH
summary: How long the stored value is, in bytes. A missing key replies nil, not zero, so nil and zero mean different things here.

name: LFRONT
summary: Reads the entry at the low end of the list without removing it. A missing or empty list replies nil. LPUSH and RPUSH are reversed relative to Redis, so the front is the opposite end from the one a Redis user would expect.

name: LINSERT
summary: Finds the first element equal to pivot and puts value beside it. A middle insert shifts everything after that point up by one. Inserting at an end is the same as LPUSH or RPUSH. A missing key replies 0, a missing pivot replies -1, and a name holding something else is WRONGTYPE.
example:
RPUSH l a b c
:3
LINSERT l BEFORE c zz
:4
LRANGE l 0 -1
*4
$1
a
$1
b
$2
zz
$1
c

name: LLEN
summary: How many entries are in the list. A missing list replies 0.

name: LMOVE
summary: Pops one element from source and pushes it onto destination. The two sides are independent. Both keys are locked by shard number, never by argument order, and the value is copied out before the destination is written. The same name is one lock. A missing source replies nil and leaves the destination alone.
example:
RPUSH src a b c
:3
LMOVE src dst RIGHT LEFT
$1
c
LRANGE dst 0 -1
*1
$1
c

name: LMPOP
summary: Pops from the first of several lists that has anything. One key locks its shard; several lock the space, as BLPOP does. COUNT defaults to 1 and must be at least 1. A name holding a string or another collection is WRONGTYPE.
example:
RPUSH l a b
:2
LMPOP 1 l LEFT COUNT 1
*2
$1
l
*1
$1
a

name: LOAD
summary: Reloads every shard of the current space from its data files, overwriting what is in memory. Destructive, and in the dangerous ACL category.

name: LOADFS
summary: Imports a directory tree from the server's filesystem into this space's file store, under root. The path is resolved by the server, not the client, so it is the server's disk that is read. Only ever adds and overwrites: a file the directory no longer has stays in the space, so the space is the union of every import run against it rather than a mirror of the directory. See Loading a directory into a space for why, and for how to make a space match a directory.
example:
USE docsdemo
+OK
LOADFS /tmp/demo /files
files=2
bytes=10
keys=2
root=/files
chunk=65536

name: LOADKEYS
summary: The same directory, imported as ordinary keys instead of as files. A file becomes the key prefix:dir:name and a .luau file becomes a stored function, which is why this carries the function category as well and why storing one runs its chunk. Additive in the same way LOADFS is: nothing is ever deleted by an import.
example:
USE docsdemo2
+OK
LOADKEYS /tmp/demo app
functions=1
keys=2
bytes=56
prefix=app

name: LPOP
summary: Removes up to count entries from the high end of the list. The count is required. The reply is the length left, not the values removed, so read them first if you need them. A missing or empty list replies nil.

name: LPUSH
summary: Pushes values onto the head of the list, creating it if needed. Several values are pushed left to right, so the last one given ends up first, as in Redis.

name: LPUSHX
summary: Pushes values onto the head only if the list already exists. A missing list is not created. The reply is 0.
example:
LPUSHX nolist a
:0
EXISTS nolist
:0
RPUSH l a
:1
LPUSHX l b
:2

name: LRANGE
summary: The elements between two positions, both ends included. Positions start at 0; a negative counts back from the end, so 0 -1 is the whole list. Positions past either end are clamped. A start past the end replies with an empty array.
example:
RPUSH l a
:1
RPUSH l b
:2
LRANGE l 0 -1
*2
$1
a
$1
b

name: MAX
summary: The last key in key order. An empty space replies nil.

name: MGET
summary: Reads several keys at once. Missing keys come back as nils in the same positions, so the reply always has one entry per key.

name: MIN
summary: The first key in key order. An empty space replies nil.

name: MOVE
summary: Moves a key into another key space, removing it from this one. A destination that already holds the name is refused and nothing moves. The db is a number, resolved to a space name the way SELECT resolves it.
example:
SET a 1
+OK
MOVE a 1
:1
EXISTS a
:0

name: MSET
summary: Sets several key/value pairs. Each pair is written under its own lock, so MSET is not atomic across keys and a reader can see some pairs applied and not others.

name: MSETNX
summary: Sets several keys, but only if every one of them is missing. If any key already exists, nothing is written. All or none.
example:
MSETNX a 1 b 2
:1
MSETNX b 3 c 4
:0
GET c
$-1

name: MULTI
summary: Opens a transaction block. Commands sent after it are queued until EXEC. Registered as write with no data category, so it is not itself replicated.

name: NEXT
summary: The first key strictly after the one given, in key order. An alias of UB, and the companion to FIRST when stepping through a range by hand.

name: OPS
summary: The operation counters — inserts, retrievals, deletes, iterations and the rest — as name and value pairs.

name: PERSIST
summary: Removes the expiry and keeps the value. Replies 0 if the key is missing or already has no expiry.
example:
SET a 1 EX 100
+OK
PERSIST a
:1
TTL a
:-1
PERSIST a
:0

name: PEXPIRE
summary: Sets how long the key should live, in milliseconds. The NX/XX/GT/LT conditions work the same as EXPIRE. A time that has already passed deletes the key.
example:
SET a 1
+OK
PEXPIRE a 50000
:1
PTTL a
:50000

name: PEXPIREAT
summary: Sets the expiry to a unix time in milliseconds. A time that has already passed deletes the key.

name: PEXPIRETIME
summary: When the key will expire, as a unix time in milliseconds.

name: PING
summary: The Redis health check. With no argument it replies PONG; with one it echoes the message back. This is what clients and connection pools send. It is not RPING.

name: PREPEND
summary: Adds bytes to the start of the stored value, creating the key if it is missing. A compressed value is stored back uncompressed, same as APPEND.

name: PSETEX
summary: SETEX with the lifetime in milliseconds. The number must be greater than zero.

name: PTTL
summary: How many milliseconds are left before the key expires. Missing keys and keys with no expiry use the same -1 and -2 as TTL.
example:
SET a 1
+OK
PEXPIRE a 50000
:1
PTTL a
:50000
TTL a
:50

name: PUBLISH
summary: Starts publishing this space's writes to the named destination.

name: PULL
summary: Adds an upstream source that this space resolves misses against. A space with a pull source is left off the ordered range-sharding fast paths and is never rebalanced, because keys it answers for may live upstream. In the dangerous ACL category.

name: QUEUE
summary: Put a message on a declared queue, or report every queue. PUSH replies with the sequence the message was given, which is the same number the handler sees, so a sender and a handler can talk about the same message even though delivery is at-least-once. A publish that cannot reach the file is an error, not a quiet zero. The queue has to have been declared first: SETF a transport() of kind queue under configuration:queues/. STATUS is the same text FUNCTIONS QUEUES prints.
example:
QUEUE PUSH work hello
:1
QUEUE STATUS
declared=queues/work name=work space=default call=TAKE user=default enabled=on durability=each max_attempts=3 waiting=0 delivered=1 failed=0 dead=0 running=no
QUEUE PUSH nosuch x
-ERR no queue called 'nosuch' is declared under configuration:queues/

name: RANDOMKEY
summary: A key chosen at random from the current key space, or nil when the space is empty. Successive calls are not guaranteed to differ, and the distribution is not promised to be uniform.

name: RELOAD
summary: Reloads this space from another server over the replication protocol. Destructive, and in the dangerous ACL category.

name: REM
summary: Removes one key and replies with the value it held. A missing key is not an error; the reply is nil. This is the barch spelling. DEL is the Redis one and replies with a count.

name: REMF
summary: Remove the function named name. Replies 1 if it was there, 0 if not; removing it twice is not an error. GET, SET and DEL cannot address a function key. RELOAD publishes the removal so connections that already compiled it stop using it on the next call; without it they keep what they compiled. Exposed RESP names declared by that function go with it.
example:
SETF greet "function call() return 1 end"
+OK
REMF greet
:1
GETF greet
$-1
REMF greet
:0

name: REMROUTE
summary: Removes a destination previously added with ADDROUTE. Removing one that is not there is not an error.

name: RENAME
summary: Moves a value from one name to another, replacing the destination if it is already there. A missing source is an error. The two names may live on different shards, and may be in different key spaces.
example:
SET a 1
+OK
RENAME a b
+OK
GET b
$1
1

name: RENAMENX
summary: RENAME that will not replace an existing destination. A missing source is still an error. An occupied destination replies 0 and leaves both names alone.
example:
SET a 1
+OK
SET b 2
+OK
RENAMENX a b
:0

name: RETRIEVE
summary: Fetches a block of data from another server. Destructive, and in the dangerous ACL category.

name: ROUTE
summary: Reports the route configuration. Host and port are required; calling it bare does not list every route.

name: RPING
summary: Opens a connection to another barch over the binary replication protocol and checks it answers. This is not PING. PING is the health check a Redis client sends about the server it is already connected to. RPING says nothing about the server being asked.

name: RPOP
summary: Removes up to count entries from the low end of the list. The count is required. The reply is the length left, not the values removed, so read them first if you need them. A missing or empty list replies nil.

name: RPOPLPUSH
summary: LMOVE source destination RIGHT LEFT. Same two-key lock order, same copy-before-write.
example:
RPUSH src a b c
:3
RPOPLPUSH src dst
$1
c

name: RPUSH
summary: Pushes values onto the tail of the list, creating it if needed, in the order they are given.

name: RPUSHX
summary: Pushes values onto the tail only if the list already exists. A missing list is not created. The reply is 0.

name: SAVE
summary: Writes the current key space to its data files. If some shards fail to write, the reply is an error, but the shards that did write are still written.

name: SAVEALL
summary: As SAVE, across every key space, not only the selected one.

name: SCAN
summary: Walks the key space a page at a time in allocation order. Start with cursor 0; the reply carries the next cursor, and 0 when the walk is done. A cursor left half-finished holds a page buffer until the connection closes. CLIENT INFO reports them as iters; CLIENT CLEAR_ITERS frees them.

name: SELECT
summary: Selects a database by number, or a key space by name. A number is mapped to a space named by db_number_prefix plus the number — db1, db2 and so on — and 0 is the default space. A name selects that space directly. Barch has named key spaces; Redis has a fixed set of numbered databases. The two do not line up exactly.
example:
SELECT 0
+OK
SELECT 1
+OK        # the space db1
SELECT events
+OK   # the space events

name: SET
syntax: SET key value [GET] [NX|XX] [EX s|PX ms|EXAT ts|PXAT ts] [KEEPTTL]
summary: Stores a value at a key. NX writes only if the key is missing; XX writes only if it is already there. A refused condition replies nil and stores nothing. Options have to appear in the order shown: SET k v NX GET is a syntax error, SET k v GET NX is fine.
example:
SET a 1
+OK
SET a 2 GET
$1 1      # the previous value
SET a 3 NX
$-1       # a is already there, nothing written

name: SETEX
summary: Sets the key and its expiry in one step, so there is no window where the key exists with no deadline. The seconds must be greater than zero. Note the argument order: the value comes last.
example:
SETEX se 100 v
+OK
TTL se
:100
SETEX se2 0 v
-ERR invalid expire time in 'setex' command

name: SETF
summary: Compile a Luau script and store it as a function key under name. The source is compiled before anything is written, so a script that will not run is refused rather than saved as a command that cannot work. Names fold to upper case and must not contain a dot. A name that is already a builtin is allowed: SET stays SET, and the stored one is reached as CALLF SET or SPACE.SET. Without RELOAD, connections that have already compiled this name keep what they have; with it the change is published to every session on its next call. AOT compiles it to native code as well, and a native miss just runs interpreted. The flag is only held in memory, so a restart or a later SETF without it drops it. A --!native line in the comments at the top of the source asks for the same thing and is kept with it, so that's the one that lasts.
example:
SETF greet "function call(who) return \"hello \" .. who end"
+OK
GETF greet
$45
function call(who) return "hello " .. who end
SETF greet "function call() return 1 end" RELOAD
+OK

name: SETNX
summary: Sets a key only if it does not already exist. An existing key keeps the value it had. The reply says which happened; it is not an error.
example:
SETNX a 1
:1
SETNX a 2
:0
GET a
$1
1

name: SETRANGE
summary: Writes bytes into the stored value starting at offset, growing it if needed. A missing key counts as empty. An offset past the end is padded with zeros, so you can build a value out of order. Writing nothing to a missing key creates nothing and replies 0. A compressed value is stored back uncompressed, same as APPEND.
example:
SET k "Hello World"
+OK
SETRANGE k 6 Redis
:11
GET k
$11 Hello Redis

name: SIZE
summary: How many keys are in the current key space. It takes read locks only, so writers are not held up.

name: SIZEALL
summary: The total key count across every key space, not just the selected one.

name: SPACES
summary: Lists the key spaces that exist and how many keys each holds. The default space is reported as (default).

name: START
summary: Starts the replication listener on the given interface and port.

name: STATS
summary: The full statistics set as name and value pairs, including range_shard_keys_moved and the memory counters.

name: STOP
summary: Stops a replication listener started with START.

name: STRLEN
summary: How long the value is, in bytes. A missing key replies 0, not nil, so you cannot tell an empty value from an absent key with this command alone. A key holding a collection is the wrong type.
example:
SET a hello
+OK
STRLEN a
:5
STRLEN nope
:0

name: SUBSTR
summary: The old name for GETRANGE. Same handler, same behaviour. Clients still send it.

name: TRAIN
summary: Adds a sample to the compression dictionary training set, or with no argument finishes training and saves the dictionary. At least five samples are wanted. Training is optional: with compression on and no training data, values are used as their own samples and a dictionary is saved automatically.

name: TTL
summary: How many seconds are left before the key expires. -1 means the key exists with no expiry; -2 means the key is missing.
example:
TTL a
:-1      # exists, no expiry
TTL nope
:-2     # no such key

name: UB
summary: The first key strictly after the given one. Replies nil if the given key is the last one.

name: UDECRBY
summary: Subtracts the given amount, reading the value as an unsigned 64-bit integer. A non-integer is left as it was and the reply is an error.

name: UINCRBY
summary: Adds the given amount, reading the value as an unsigned 64-bit integer. A non-integer is left as it was and the reply is an error.

name: UNLOAD
summary: Closes a key space and releases the memory its shards hold. The data on disk is left alone, so the space comes back on the next USE.

name: USE
summary: Selects the named key space for this connection. With no argument, or with the name 0, it returns to the default space. A space that does not exist is created, and it reads its configuration once when first built. USE only ever takes a name, so it is how you reach a space whose name happens to be a number — SELECT would read that as a database.

name: ZADD
summary: Adds members with scores to an ordered set, creating it if needed. An existing member has its score replaced.

name: ZCARD
summary: How many members are in the set. A missing set replies 0.

name: ZCOUNT
summary: Counts members whose scores fall between two bounds, without returning them.

name: ZDIFF
summary: Members of the first set that are not in the others. The numkeys count comes first and must match the number of keys that follow, as in Redis.

name: ZDIFFSTORE
summary: Stores the difference of the given sets in a destination key. This does not yet agree with Redis on the result — see the warning on set algebra.

name: ZFASTRANK
summary: The same question as ZRANK, answered in constant time from trace paths and node counts on the radix tree. Prefer it over ZRANK on wide ranges. The two agree on the answer.

name: ZINCRBY
summary: Adds an amount to a member's score, creating the member at that score if it is missing.

name: ZINTER
summary: Members present in every named set.

name: ZINTERCARD
summary: Counts the members present in every named set without returning them.

name: ZINTERSTORE
summary: Stores the intersection of the given sets in a destination key. This does not yet agree with Redis on the result, and WEIGHTS and AGGREGATE are not applied — see the warning on set algebra.

name: ZMPOP
summary: Pops from the first of several ordered sets that has anything. Each pop removes both the score key and the member index, which is what ZREM does and what ZPOPMIN and ZPOPMAX still do not. COUNT defaults to 1. A name holding a string or another collection is WRONGTYPE.
example:
ZADD z 1 a 2 b 3 c
:3
ZMPOP 1 z MIN
*2
$1
z
*1
*2
$1
a
$1
1

name: ZMSCORE
summary: The scores of several members at once, in the order they were asked for. A missing member contributes nil, so the reply lines up with the request.

name: ZPOPMAX
summary: Removes and returns the member with the highest score, member first and score second, as Redis does. An empty set replies with an empty array.

name: ZPOPMIN
summary: Removes and returns the member with the lowest score, member first and score second, as Redis does. An empty set replies with an empty array.

name: ZRANDMEMBER
summary: Picks a member at random. With no count, one member comes back, or nil if the set is missing. A positive count asks for that many distinct members; a negative count allows repeats. As with HRANDFIELD, a count past a million is refused because the reply is built in memory first.

name: ZRANGE
syntax: ZRANGE key start stop [BYSCORE | BYLEX] [REV] [LIMIT offset count] [WITHSCORES]
summary: Members between two positions. Positions start at 0; a negative counts back from the end, so ZRANGE key 0 -1 is the whole set. Out-of-range positions are clamped. BYSCORE or BYLEX reads the bounds as scores or lex bounds instead, and only then is LIMIT allowed. A position or a LIMIT offset is reached by jumping, so a page deep into a large set costs about what the first page does. REV with a LIMIT still reads the whole range and slices it.
example:
ZRANGE z 0 -1
1) "m1"
2) "m2"
ZRANGE z 1000 1009
# ten members from position 1000, without reading the first 1000
ZRANGE z -inf +inf BYSCORE LIMIT 1000 10

name: ZRANGEBYLEX
syntax: ZRANGEBYLEX key min max [LIMIT offset count]
summary: Members between two lexical bounds. As in Redis this only makes sense when every member shares a score; when scores differ the order is by score and the answer will not be a lexical read. LIMIT offset count leaves out the first offset members in range and returns up to count, jumping to the offset rather than reading up to it.

name: ZRANGEBYSCORE
syntax: ZRANGEBYSCORE key min max [WITHSCORES] [LIMIT offset count]
summary: Members whose scores fall between two bounds, in ascending score order. ( in front of a bound makes it exclusive. LIMIT offset count leaves out the first offset members in range and returns up to count; the offset is reached by the counts in the tree rather than by reading the members before it. An empty range replies with an empty array.

name: ZRANK
summary: Counts members between two bounds. This is not Redis ZRANK, which takes a key and one member and reports that member's position. Here the command takes two bounds and replies with how many members lie between them. An inverted range replies 0. See ZFASTRANK for the constant-time form.

name: ZREM
summary: Removes members from an ordered set. Missing members are skipped.

name: ZREMRANGEBYLEX
summary: Removes members between two lexical bounds. An empty range removes nothing and is not an error.

name: ZREMRANGEBYSCORE
summary: Removes every member whose score falls between the two bounds, both included. A bound that is not a number is refused. Removing a member takes both of its keys — the score-ordered one and its entry in the member index — so ZSCORE and ZRANK stay consistent afterwards.
example:
ZADD z 1 a 2 b 3 c
:3
ZREMRANGEBYSCORE z 2 3
:2
ZRANGE z 0 -1
*1
$1
a

name: ZREVRANGE
summary: As ZRANGE, walking from the high end down. The bounds can be scores, same as ZRANGE.

name: ZREVRANGEBYLEX
summary: As ZRANGEBYLEX, walking from the high end down.

name: ZREVRANGEBYSCORE
syntax: ZREVRANGEBYSCORE key max min [WITHSCORES] [LIMIT offset count]
summary: As ZRANGEBYSCORE, walking from the high score down. With a LIMIT it reads the whole range and slices it, so a deep offset here is not the jump ZRANGEBYSCORE makes.

name: ZSCORE
summary: The score a member holds. A missing member, or a missing set, replies nil. This reads the member index directly.
example:
ZADD z 1.5 a
:1
ZSCORE z a
$3
1.5
ZSCORE z nope
$-1

name: ZUNION
summary: Every member of any of the given sets. A member's score is what AGGREGATE does with the scores it had in each set, after each of those was multiplied by that set's weight. Members come back in score order, and by member where scores tie.
example:
ZADD a 1 x
:1
ZADD b 2 y
:1
ZUNION 2 a b WITHSCORES
*4
$1
x
$1
1
$1
y
$1
2

name: ZUNIONSTORE
syntax: ZUNIONSTORE destination numkeys key [key ...] [WEIGHTS w [w ...]] [AGGREGATE SUM|MIN|MAX]
summary: What ZUNION would return, written to a destination key instead. The destination is replaced, not added to. WITHSCORES is a syntax error here.
